newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin leaves sanatorium as budget worries mount.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin leaves sanatorium as budget worries mount.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, facing a miners' strikes and problems with the 1997 budget, left a sanatorium for a country residence on Wednesday almost exactly a month after undergoing major heart surgery.

The Kremlin said Yeltsin, who had his operation on November 5, had moved to an official residence at Gorky-9, a village near Moscow where many top officials have country homes that lies up the road from the Barvikha sanatorium.
Doctors expect him to be back at his Kremlin desk towards the end of this month and to start paying brief visits to his office before that.
Yeltsin, 65, has been meeting officials at the Barvikha sanatorium, although he has appeared only rarely on television.
He met Prime Minister Vitkor Chernomyrdin on Wednesday, discussing issues like a European security summit held earlier this week and the 1997 budget, due to be discussed by parliament on Friday.

The State Duma lower house of parliament, dominated by communists and their conservative allies, on Wednesday approved new tax legislation and passed a resolution criticising Yeltsin's decree pulling troops out of breakaway Chechnya.
The Duma asked Yeltsin to withdraw his decision and take all measures needed to provide security in the northern Caucasus.

A campaign for a presidential election in Chechnya has already started and Russian news agencies on Wednesday quoted Chechen information minister Movladi Udugov as saying that he would stand. The vote is due on January 27.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which held a summit in Lisbon this week, helped broker the peace deal.
The Russian Foreign Ministry, ignoring Moscow's isolation on several issues at the meeting, hailed the two-day summit as a triumph for its ideas on future European security.
"The main result of the summit is that our idea for creating a new model of European security is winning ever more support," a ministry statement said.
But the Russian team failed to win support for a proposal to develop the OSCE into a powerful security body or to change Western views on the need to expand the NATO defence alliance.
Chernomyrdin returned home from Lisbon to a row about next year's state budget and a miners' strike.
The miners helped Yeltsin to electoral success in 1991. Now, impoverished by his free market economic reforms and bitter at mounting wage arrears, they want his government to quit.
The miners blame the government for the web of wage and tax arrears, one of Russia's biggest social and economic problems.
Union officials said 400,000 miners were taking industrial action on Wednesday, the second day of the strike. But coal company Rosugol said only 61,000 mine workers had downed tools.

Interfax news agency said Chernomyrdin and Yeltsin had decided to send First Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin to the main mining region -- the southern Siberian region of the Kuzbass -- to talk to the miners there.
Another economic problem facing the government is the fate of Russia's 1997 budget draft.
Parliament has already rejected the draft once, complaining that revenue plans are unrealistic and spending forecasts do not take the needs of the poorest Russians into account.

Chernomyrdin is due to attend Friday's Duma debate, but, pleading he was feeling unwell, he turned down an invitation from the Federation Council upper house on Wednesday. Some deputies, clearly angry, said the chamber should look at the possibility of a no-confidence vote in the government.
